extracted.intended_audience: general readers and writers of poetry/recitation; students of American verse and performance
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative principles for composing and selecting poems and recitations meant to be performed for general audiences, emphasizing natural voice, audience response, dialect, and performancecraft.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naturalness / Authenticity
rubrics_metrics.description: “The public desires nothing but what is absolutely natural, and so perfectly natural as to be fairly artless. It can not tolerate affectation, and it takes little interest in the classical production. It demands simple sentiments that come direct from the heart.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write in an unaffected, artless manner; favor simple, heartfelt sentiments over affected or overly 'classical' language. Authenticity of feeling and voice is prioritized; avoid mannered or artificial stylistic flourishes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience responsiveness / engagement
rubrics_metrics.description: Riley watched the effect his readings had on the audience: “whenever anybody left the hall I knew that my recitation was at fault and tried to find out why.” He judged and valued his verses by their effect upon the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use audience reaction as a test: attendance and attention are metrics of success. If listeners disengage, reassess choice of piece, delivery, or subject matter. Iteratively refine material based on live feedback.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of audience sensibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: After a couple left during 'The Happy Little Cripple' because they had a hunch-back child, Riley ceased using that recitation: the anecdote emphasizes being mindful of audience circumstances and sensitivities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that particular topics or scenes may cause discomfort to audience members; avoid material likely to unintentionally distress typical listeners of the venue or tailor presentation accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accessibility vs. writing 'over the heads' of the audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Riley admitted he at first 'presumed to write 'over the heads' of the audience' and later learned to dislike anything that did not appeal to the public, learning to discriminate between what did not 'ring true' to hearers and what 'won them by virtue of its truthfulness and was simply heart high.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor clarity, directness, and emotional resonance appropriate to the intended audience over intellectual display or abstruse allusion. Ensure material 'rings true' to listeners rather than being needlessly obscure or elitist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be open to unexpected audience preferences
rubrics_metrics.description: A listener suggested Riley recite 'When the Frost Is on the Punkin'—which Riley had not thought suitable—and it became one of his most favored recitations. He learned to value works by their public effect, not just his own instincts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remain receptive to audience or colleague suggestions and empirical evidence of popularity; pieces you initially underestimate may become highly effective when performed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recitation structure: length, climax, and recitation-specific features
rubrics_metrics.description: On the platform Riley noted of a successful recitation: 'It fulfilled, as few poems do, all the requirements of length, climax and those many necessary features for a recitation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When selecting or composing a piece for recitation, attend to appropriate length, a clear and well-built climax, and other features that sustain listeners (rhythm, narrative arc, memorable lines). Tailor structure for spoken performance rather than only for the printed page.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authentic dialect and vernacular rooted in observation
rubrics_metrics.description: Riley's exposure to courthouse speech and local people made the dialect and native speech 'familiar to him, and took firm root in the fresh soil of his young memory.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using dialect or vernacular, base it on close observation and familiarity with the speech community; authenticity (not caricature) lends credibility and emotional truth to characters and voice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performance naturalism, simplicity, and timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Mark Twain praised Riley's rendering of the humorous story: 'The simplicity and innocence and sincerity and unconsciousness of Riley's old farmer are perfectly simulated, and the result is a performance which is thoroughly charming and delicious.' Also, Twain contrasted a one-and-a-half-minute telling with a ten-minute humorous-story version—timing and form affect comedic impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for a natural, sincere, almost unselfconscious delivery in performance; simulate simplicity and innocence where appropriate. Pay close attention to pacing and timing (expansion or compression of a story can alter its comic or emotional effect). Mastery of timing is required for the best results.
